title: What training does Food Safety Standard 3.2.2A require?
description: What Food Standards Code Standard 3.2.2A requires for food handler training and food safety supervisors, which businesses it covers, and what records help.
shortAnswer: Food Standards Code Standard 3.2.2A, in force in Australia since 8 December 2023, requires category one and category two food service, catering and retail businesses to ensure each food handler of unpackaged, potentially hazardous, ready to eat food has completed a food safety training course or has equivalent skills and knowledge, and to appoint a certified food safety supervisor whose certificate is less than five years old.
keyTakeaways: Standard 3.2.2A commenced 12 months after gazettal, on 8 December 2023, and applies to Australian category one and category two food businesses.
Section 3.2.2A-10 requires food handlers doing a prescribed activity to have completed a food safety training course, or have commensurate skills and knowledge, before starting.
A food safety training course must cover safe handling of food, food contamination, cleaning and sanitising, and personal hygiene.
Section 3.2.2A-11 requires a food safety supervisor certified within the previous 5 years, reasonably available to advise and supervise food handlers.
Category one businesses must also keep records substantiating critical controls for 3 months, unless they can demonstrate compliance another way.
jurisdiction: Australia: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code, Standard 3.2.2A (Australia only), enforced under state and territory food laws
regulator: Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) develops the standard; state and territory food regulators enforce it
appliesTo: Category one businesses: caterers and food service businesses that process unpackaged potentially hazardous food into ready to eat potentially hazardous food
Category two businesses: retailers of potentially hazardous, ready to eat food handled unpackaged but not made on site
Food handlers engaged in prescribed activities

sections.heading: Which businesses does Standard 3.2.2A apply to?

blocks.text: Standard 3.2.2A applies to Australian food businesses that are category one or category two businesses, which in practice means food service, catering and retail businesses handling unpackaged, potentially hazardous food that is ready to eat. [FSANZ](https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/food-safety/overview-food-safety-management-tools) gives caterers, restaurants, cafes, takeaway shops, pubs, supermarkets, delis and food vans as typical examples.

blocks.caption: Categories under Standard 3.2.2A, sections 3.2.2A-6 to 3.2.2A-9
head: Category
Definition (summary)
Tools required
rows: Category one
A caterer or food service business that processes unpackaged potentially hazardous food into food that is both potentially hazardous and ready to eat
Food handler training (3.2.2A-10), food safety supervisor (3.2.2A-11), substantiation records (3.2.2A-12)
Category two

A business that sells potentially hazardous, ready to eat food that was received or handled unpackaged but not made or processed on site, other than slicing, weighing, repacking, reheating or hot holding
Food handler training (3.2.2A-10), food safety supervisor (3.2.2A-11)

blocks.text: The standard does not apply to handling food for or at a fund raising event. All food businesses, whether or not covered by 3.2.2A, must still comply with Standards 3.2.2 and 3.2.3, including the general requirement in clause 3 of [Standard 3.2.2](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2008B00576/latest/text) that people undertaking or supervising food handling have skills and knowledge in food safety and food hygiene commensurate with their work.

Standard 3.2.2A commenced on 8 December 2023. The instrument on the [Federal Register of Legislation](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2022L01589/latest/text) was made in December 2022 and states that it commences on a date 12 months after gazettal; the as made version is dated 8 December 2022.

The Food Standards Code is developed by Food Standards Australia New Zealand (FSANZ) and applied through each state and territory's food legislation, so enforcement, certificate recognition and some practical arrangements are handled by the local food regulator. This page reflects the standard and FSANZ guidance as at September 2026.

sections.heading: What does food handler training under section 3.2.2A-10 require?

blocks.text: Every food handler who engages in a prescribed activity must, before starting that activity, either have completed a food safety training course or have skills and knowledge of food safety and hygiene commensurate with the specific activity. A prescribed activity is handling unpackaged potentially hazardous food that is used to prepare ready to eat food for consumers, or is ready to eat food for retail sale.

blocks.title: Primary text: Standard 3.2.2A, definition of food safety training course
blocks.text: "food safety training course means training in food safety that includes training in each of the following: (a) safe handling of food; and (b) food contamination; and (c) cleaning and sanitising of food premises and equipment; and (d) personal hygiene."

The standard does not name a provider, format or duration. [FSANZ's food handler training guidance](https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/food-safety/food-handler-training) says no specific refresher period has been set, but businesses must make sure food handlers' skills and knowledge stay adequate and up to date, and regular refresher training is best practice. It also says a business can recognise prior learning, such as competency based training, in house education or an induction completed at another food business, and relevant industry experience.

Because the alternative to a course is demonstrated skills and knowledge, a short [competency assessment](/glossary/competency-assessment) is often the most practical way to recognise an experienced worker. FSANZ notes that keeping records of training is optional under this section but helps a business show authorised officers it has met the requirement.

sections.heading: What training does a food safety supervisor need?

blocks.text: The food safety supervisor must hold a food safety supervisor certificate issued within the immediately preceding five years and have the authority and ability to manage and give direction on safe food handling. The certificate must come from a registered training organisation or an organisation recognised by the relevant food regulator.

Section 3.2.2A-11 requires the business to appoint the supervisor before engaging in a prescribed activity and ensure the supervisor is reasonably available to advise and supervise each food handler. [FSANZ](https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/food-safety/food-safety-supervisor) explains that reasonably available means working on site or being easily contactable, and that appointing someone who does not regularly handle food or is never on site is not considered reasonable.

items: Ensure food safety risks are managed and issues are prevented or corrected.
Instruct staff, review and update business procedures, and inspect premises and food handling operations.
Share food safety knowledge with other food handlers.
Foster a positive food safety culture.

blocks.text: Competency units for the supervisor course are listed on training.gov.au. FSANZ notes that some providers offer refresher courses; otherwise the full course must be repeated every five years. Because the certificate expires, supervisor renewal dates belong in the business's [training matrix](/glossary/training-matrix) with a reminder well before the five year point.

sections.heading: How does the evidence tool relate to training?

blocks.text: Category one businesses must make records that substantiate their management of prescribed activities and keep them for three months, unless they can demonstrate compliance to an authorised officer another way. The link to training is direct: one alternative FSANZ recognises is training staff on a standard operating procedure and walking an authorised officer through it.

The [FSANZ evidence tool guidance](https://www.foodstandards.gov.au/business/food-safety/evidence-tool) lists acceptable records such as entries on paper or electronic templates, verified written instructions such as a validated recipe or [standard operating procedure](/glossary/standard-operating-procedure), temperature notes on invoices, data logger output, and photos or video. A trained food handler who can physically demonstrate an activity, such as sanitising equipment or measuring food temperature, can also substantiate compliance.

sections.heading: What does a compliant training record look like?

blocks.text: A compliant record shows who handles high risk food, what training or recognised experience covers each of the four required topics, and who the certified supervisor is. The table below is an illustrative template; businesses should adapt it to their own activities and regulator.

blocks.text: Recording the training date before the handler's first shift on high risk food shows the "before engaging in that activity" requirement was met. For broader methods, see [how to structure onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles) and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps the four required training topics and each site procedure to defined learning outcomes and assessment points, so a multi site food business can show which handler was assessed on which procedure version and when. Supervisor certificate expiry is tracked as a competence requirement. See [operational procedure programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Do food handlers need a certificate to meet Standard 3.2.2A?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Section 3.2.2A-10 accepts either a completed food safety training course or skills and knowledge commensurate with the prescribed activity. FSANZ says businesses can recognise prior learning and relevant experience. The food safety supervisor, by contrast, must hold a certificate issued within the previous five years.

faqs.q: How often must food handler training be refreshed?
faqs.a: The standard sets no refresher period for food handlers. FSANZ says businesses must keep handlers' skills and knowledge adequate and up to date and describes regular refresher training as best practice. Food safety supervisor certification must be renewed so that it is never more than five years old.

faqs.q: Can one food safety supervisor cover several sites?
faqs.a: The standard requires the supervisor to be reasonably available to advise and supervise each food handler engaged in a prescribed activity. FSANZ says that means working on site or being easily contactable, and that someone who is never on site is not a reasonable appointment. Businesses should check local regulator guidance for multi site arrangements.

faqs.q: Does Standard 3.2.2A apply in New Zealand?
faqs.a: No. Section 3.2.2A-3 applies the standard to food businesses in Australia that are category one or category two businesses. New Zealand has its own food safety framework.

factCheck.claim: Standard 3.2.2A commences 12 months after gazettal; as made version dated 8 December 2022, giving commencement on 8 December 2023; FSANZ says requirements came in December 2023.
Food safety training course is defined as training in safe handling of food, food contamination, cleaning and sanitising of premises and equipment, and personal hygiene.

Section 3.2.2A-10 requires handlers in a prescribed activity to have completed a course or have commensurate skills and knowledge before engaging in that activity; 3.2.2A-11 requires appointing a supervisor who is reasonably available.

Food safety supervisor means a person holding a certificate issued within the preceding 5 years, from an RTO or an organisation recognised by the relevant authority, with authority and ability to direct safe food handling.
Section 3.2.2A-12 requires category one businesses to make substantiating records and keep them for 3 months.
FSANZ: no specific refresher period has been set for food handler training; regular refresher training is best practice; prior learning and experience can be recognised.
Standard 3.2.2 clause 3 requires persons undertaking or supervising food handling operations to have skills and knowledge in food safety and hygiene commensurate with their work.
